title: Claim Charts for Patent Litigation: Comprehensive Outline (Software Litigation Consulting)

extracted.subtask_short: All-elements rule, pinpoint citations, failure-pattern taxonomy
extracted.subtask_description: A comprehensive outline of claim-chart requirements: the all-elements/each-x3 comprehensiveness rule, location-specificity standards, claim disaggregation, right-column content requirements, evidence standards by litigation stage, and a taxonomy of problematic chart patterns (mimicking, laundry-list, Frankencharts, dumping, information-and-belief overreliance, inventor's fallacy) used to judge whether a mapping is a genuine match or a stretch.

rubrics_metrics.name: All-elements rule — no "NOPed" limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts must identify "specifically and in detail where each element of each asserted claim is found within each accused instrumentality" (the same standard applies, mutatis mutandis, to invalidity charts against prior art): each claim limitation requires explicit treatment, each asserted claim requires separate analysis, each accused product/reference requires mapping. No elements may be "NOPed" (dropped via "not operating present") — a single unaddressed or unmatched limitation defeats the theory (whether infringement or invalidity/anticipation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Location specificity — pinpoint citations required
rubrics_metrics.description: "Specifically where" mandates factual equivalents to legal "pinpoint" citations. Reviewing courts/panels reject mere assertions ("it's in there"), inferred presence without evidence, and vague references ("See document X"). Acceptable pinpointing examples: source code line numbers, filenames with pathnames, product version numbers, functional component names with brief descriptions, and — for prior art — column:line citations, figure numbers, and specific passages of a reference document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim disaggregation beyond semicolons
rubrics_metrics.description: Semicolons typically delimit major limitations, but only as a "first approximation." Identifying all limitations requires examining explicit clauses beginning with "wherein"; preambles (often limiting despite conventional wisdom that they are not); preconditions and "whereby" clauses; implicit sub-limitations emerging from claim structure; negative limitations ("without," "substantially free of"); functional language under 35 U.S.C. § 112(f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural analysis: identify the attributes/facets along which parts can be compared (e.g., function/way/result, used originally for the Doctrine of Equivalents but useful more generally for judging whether a mapping is a genuine match).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right column content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts presented in the mapping column must: (1) assert explicitly what connection exists between right-column facts and left-column limitations; (2) explain "why" the facts support the assertion (not proof, but a reasoned basis); (3) interweave fact language with construed limitation language (not mere side-by-side juxtaposition); (4) isolate presence of each limitation within the accused instrumentality/reference — avoid "dumping" pages of undifferentiated material; (5) avoid assumptions about operation from external appearance or output alone (the "inventor's fallacy").

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence requirements by litigation stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-discovery (preliminary infringement contentions / initial invalidity contentions) must reflect "reverse engineering or its equivalent," require exhaustion of publicly accessible information, may invoke "information and belief" only after diligent investigation, and should identify what information remains unavailable despite diligence. Post-discovery (final contentions) require enhanced specificity and granularity: source code citations with pathname/filename/line numbers or function names, detailed explanation of why code structure (or reference disclosure) satisfies claim limitations, and claim construction explicitly applied in the fact comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Mimicking" charts — merely repeat claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: "Mimicking" charts merely repeat claim language and fail to describe the accused instrumentality (or reference) in its own terms and nomenclature.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Laundry list" charts — disconnected parts without interoperation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Laundry list" charts present disconnected parts/elements without showing how they interoperate as required by the claim structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak — elements present individually but not shown combined as claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Frankencharts" — assembling limitations from incompatible modes
rubrics_metrics.description: "Frankencharts" assemble one limitation from one product mode/embodiment and another limitation from an incompatible mode — creating a non-functional combination that was never actually practiced or disclosed as a unified whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fatal flaw, especially for anticipation, where a single reference must disclose the elements as an integrated, operable whole, not stitched from separate teachings.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Dumping" charts — undifferentiated excerpts without pinpointing
rubrics_metrics.description: "Dumping" charts juxtapose claim language with massive undifferentiated source-code or document excerpts lacking pinpoint citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Information and belief" overreliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Asserting facts as "I&B" without explaining what reasonable investigation was conducted or why it proved insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Inventor's fallacy" — inferring structure from output or naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferring internal operation/structure from product output or naming conventions without examination of the actual implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weak — a stretch, since the surface label does not establish the underlying structure/function required by the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong chart entry standard (contrast to failure patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong chart entry, by contrast, cites a specific location, quotes/paraphrases the actual disclosure, and explains — using the construed claim term — why that specific disclosure satisfies (not just resembles) the limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction integration in charting
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim charts must employ the construed claim language, not merely unconstrued statutory text: identify the features/attributes the construction emphasizes; compare each construed-limitation attribute against the corresponding accused-instrumentality/reference attribute; use the construction to structure the comparison, not as an afterthought. For pre-Markman charts, adopt some reasonable provisional construction (not mere conclusory statements); post-Markman, adjust charts to reflect the court's construction while identifying any limitation's presence under multiple construction alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents charting (Function/Way/Result)
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting DoE, charts must explain, per limitation: Function (the role/purpose the limitation performs in the system), Way (the implementation/means/mechanism employed), Result (the output/effect achieved). Beyond F/W/R, charts may reference additional equivalence factors: known interchangeability, evidence of copying versus design-around, industry practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If literal infringement exists, DoE would also apply by definition; F/W/R analysis therefore helps validate whether literal infringement itself exists, and — by extension — whether an invalidity mapping is a true anticipation match versus merely an equivalent-but-not-identical disclosure (relevant because inherency/anticipation has stricter identity requirements than DoE).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means-plus-function limitation matching (§ 112(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: Charts must identify "structure(s), act(s), or material(s) in the Accused Instrumentality [or prior-art reference] that performs the claimed function." Infringement/anticipation requires matching not just the function but the specific structure/act/material disclosed in the patent specification (or its equivalent). Merely performing the claimed function is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely performing the claimed function is a classic "stretch" mapping error; charts must show how the accused/reference structure matches or is equivalent to the specification disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative instrumentalities and dependent-claim treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: The chart must separately address additional limitations not present in the base (independent) claim for dependent claims — each dependent limitation still needs its own row and its own mapped disclosure, even though invalidity of the independent claim also invalidates dependents charted against it. Representative instrumentalities/references are permitted when charting similar product variants, but require a separate showing explaining why the charted product is representative of uncharted products; each "class" of products should have at least one charted example. "Copy & paste" repetitive charts should be avoided in favor of cross-references with explicit explanatory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment good-cause standard for claim charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Good cause requires showing: newly discovered non-public information despite earlier diligent investigation; recent product launches post-filing; information from a consultant/expert previously unavailable; materials produced in discovery not earlier publicly available; for prior art specifically, material genuinely newly discovered (a less flexible standard than for infringement contentions, since prior art should have been publicly accessible all along).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delayed amendments suggest inadequate diligence; prejudice analysis asks whether the amendment requires new investigation/expert analysis or significantly alters case theory.
